features.title: The last post from Queenstown
features.body: A letter posted in Queenstown outlived the ship it was written on. It is one of the small, personal traces of Titanic’s last call in Ireland.
features.more: Passenger Edward Colley wrote on board and posted his letter before Titanic crossed the Atlantic. Cobh Heritage Centre tells his story alongside those of photographer Fr Frank Browne and Jeremiah Burke.

features.title: A revolution, street by street
features.body: Start at St Canice’s Cathedral and the history of independence takes on the scale of a walk. Davy Holden follows the people and places that put Kilkenny into the story.
features.more: The route reaches back to the revolutions in America and France before following the Fenians, the Easter Rising and the War of Independence through the city. Davy’s tour page sets out the route and the stories behind its stops.

features.title: A ledge of their own
features.body: From the clifftop, the rock looks almost sheer. From a seabird’s perspective, the same face is a neighbourhood of ledges, each with its own tenants.
features.more: Guillemots and razorbills return early in the breeding season. Puffins arrive later. From the viewing platforms, the Great Stack and the grassy outcrop called Goats Island offer a glimpse of how the birds divide up the coast.

features.title: The stories close to home
features.body: Before the camera, there were the tunes, the stories told by older neighbours and the stones near his home. That is where Davy Holden traces the start of his work.
features.more: Davy began making Irish history videos in 2022. His biography connects the monuments around his childhood home with the workshops through which he now shares history and Gaeilge.

features.title: A harbour of departures
features.body: People arrived here by rail and left by sea. The old railway station at Cobh now holds the stories of people whose journeys took them far beyond Cork Harbour.
features.more: The Queenstown Story follows very different crossings, from forced transportation to voluntary emigration. The port makes a useful place to start a family history: a name on a passenger list was once someone standing on this shore.

features.title: How to read a sea cliff
features.body: The dark bands at the edge of County Clare were laid down long before there was an Atlantic coast here. Read upwards and the rock tells a story of water giving way to land.
features.more: The lowest exposed layers formed in deeper water. As sediment accumulated, the water grew shallower. The stack standing offshore records a much later chapter: waves wore away the rock that once joined it to the mainland.

features.title: History at walking pace
features.body: A list of names on a street-side memorial asks a different question from a date in a book. Who, from this particular place, lived through the events we remember?
features.more: On his Kilkenny walk, Davy Holden uses the city itself to trace a much larger history. Moving from one site to the next puts the distances between neighbourhoods, meeting places and memorials back into the story.

features.title: A fleet within sight of home
features.body: December 1796 brought a French expedition almost to the Irish shore. Wolfe Tone had spent months working towards this moment. Then the weather made the decision for him.
features.more: With the fleet separated and the wind against a landing, the expedition withdrew. Tone’s journals let us follow the gap between what he could see from a ship and what he was powerless to do.

features.title: The organiser from Kilkenny
features.body: Long before there was a Fenian proclamation, there was the work of finding people willing to act together. James Stephens carried that work from Kilkenny to exile and back.
features.more: The Irish Republican Brotherhood was founded on St Patrick’s Day in 1858. The Kilkenny Archaeological Society tells the local story of the man who helped create it.

features.title: An Irish cause on Canadian ground
features.body: On 2 June 1866, Canadian militia faced an unusual opponent near the Niagara frontier: Irish nationalists who had crossed the border from the United States.
features.more: The Fenian raid brought Irish revolutionary politics onto Canadian soil. Fort Erie’s museum preserves watercolours of the raid and the return of the wounded. The battlefield itself is now a national historic site.

features.title: Reading the Rising one street at a time
features.body: A map of the Easter Rising looks different when you follow a single company. On Easter Monday 1916, Seán Connolly’s group went from Liberty Hall to City Hall and the buildings beside it.
features.more: The National Library of Ireland follows their route through College Green and Dame Street. Its account of the City Hall garrison makes a short walk through central Dublin into a way of reading the events of the week.

curiosity.title: The window above the door
curiosity.body: At Newgrange, the midwinter sun enters through a small opening above the entrance. Its light travels along the passage and reaches the inner chamber.

curiosity.title: An instrument played with the elbow
curiosity.body: A piper works a bellows under one arm to fill the bag of the uilleann pipes. That leaves the player free to breathe normally while a tune runs on.

curiosity.title: A tower built to be heard
curiosity.body: Glendalough’s round tower rises about 30 metres. Its job as a bell tower helps explain why it was built to stand so far above the monastic settlement.

curiosity.title: Thirty years for a castle
curiosity.body: Hugh de Lacy and his successors took some thirty years to build Trim Castle. The keep was only one layer of defence. A wall, ditch and moat guarded the approach.

curiosity.title: When a cliff becomes an island
curiosity.body: Branaunmore, the great sea stack off the Cliffs of Moher, once belonged to the mainland. Erosion left the 67-metre pillar standing apart.

curiosity.title: A room for a tune
curiosity.body: Uilleann piping has long been taught by ear, often one player sitting beside another. A written score alone can scarcely show what the hands and elbows are doing.

sport.title: What a parish passes on
sport.body: In hurling, the skills of striking and catching travel from player to player, often within a family or local club. UNESCO recorded the game as living heritage in 2018.

sport.title: Read a final in yesterday’s paper
sport.body: A match report saves details the scoreline loses. The GAA’s archive pairs contemporary accounts of All-Ireland finals from 1913 to 1923 with team photographs.

sport.title: Croke Park, in the records
sport.body: Maps, witness statements and photographs tell the story of Bloody Sunday at Croke Park in November 1920. The GAA has gathered the records into one public archive.

sport.title: Keeping the game alive
sport.body: A hurley and a sliotar are easy to recognise. Learning to play takes a community. Clubs, schools and families keep hurling and camogie in everyday Irish life.
